What you will be able to do after this page
  1. Explain why “gradient descent on a probability measure” needs a distance rather than a subtraction, and write the JKO step α(ℓ+1)∈argminα​2τ1​W22​(α(ℓ),α)+f(α) as the implicit Euler step of the Wasserstein geometry.
  2. Compute first variations δαδf​ and Wasserstein gradients ∇W​f=∇δαδf​ of the usual energies (potential, entropy, interaction, KL, MMD, W22​), and write the limit PDE ∂t​αt​=div(αt​∇δαδf​(αt​)).
  3. Recognise the classical equations as gradient flows: transport by −∇V, the heat equation (entropy), aggregation (interaction), Fokker–Planck (KL to a Gibbs measure) — and pass from densities (Eulerian) to particles (Lagrangian) and to the Langevin SDE.
  4. Prove the rates: energy dissipation, O(1/t) for geodesically convex energies, e−2λt under λ-convexity or a Polyak–Łojasiewicz inequality; state the log-Sobolev, Talagrand and HWI inequalities and check them on Gaussians.
  5. Run particle flows of discrepancies (MMD, energy distance, Sinkhorn) and Gaussian closures (Bures–Wasserstein flows), and say what they are used for: generative modelling, sampling, variational inference.
  6. Read the training of a two-layer network as a Wasserstein gradient flow of its neurons, the layers of a transformer as interacting tokens, and single-cell time courses as snapshots of a flow.
  7. Solve every exercise of the sheet Gradient Flows — Exercises (and twelve more), and know which statements of the resources contain slips.

The story of the lesson in seven steps#

To minimise an energy over probability measures, move the mass downhill in the transport geometry: implicit steps measured by W2​ (JKO) converge to a continuity equation whose velocity is minus the gradient of the first variation; this one equation describes diffusion, sampling, particle systems, wide neural networks and transformers.

  1. The model (§1). In Rd, the gradient flow x˙=−∇h(x) is discretised either explicitly (gradient descent) or implicitly (a proximal step, a small minimisation problem). Only the implicit step makes sense with nothing but a distance.
  2. The JKO step (§2). Replace the Euclidean distance by W2​: each step finds a measure with lower energy that is close to the current one in transport distance. For a Dirac it is the proximal step; for the entropy and a Gaussian it can be computed by hand.
  3. Derivatives on measures (§3–§4). The first variation δαδf​ (perturb by mixing) is a function; its gradient ∇δαδf​ (perturb by moving) is the Wasserstein gradient. Letting τ→0 gives the PDE ∂t​αt​=div(αt​∇δαδf​): transport, heat, aggregation, Fokker–Planck.
  4. Particles and noise (§5–§6). Started from n Diracs, the flow is an ODE for n particles — exactly gradient descent on their positions, sped up by n. Energies with an entropy are not defined on particles: noise replaces them, and the Fokker–Planck flow becomes the Langevin diffusion, the engine of sampling and of diffusion models.
  5. How fast (§7). Convexity along W2​ geodesics (displacement convexity) plays the role of convexity: O(1/t) rates, and e−2λt under λ-convexity. For KL, the rate is the log-Sobolev inequality.
  6. Machine-learning energies (§8–§9). MMD, energy distance and Sinkhorn are defined on particle clouds and give generative particle flows; Gaussian families give finite-dimensional flows of means and covariances (Bures–Wasserstein), used in variational inference.
  7. Learning systems as flows of measures (§10–§12). The neurons of a wide two-layer network, the tokens of a transformer, the cells of a developing organism: three populations moving by a velocity that depends on the whole population.

What you need#

Open only the refreshers you need. Each one says exactly what is used on this page. The Reminders page has the longer versions (links), and Lesson 3 has the Wasserstein geometry.

Refresher — gradient descent, convexity, strong convexity, Grönwall

A differentiable h:Rd→R is convex if it lies above its tangents: h(y)≥h(x)+⟨∇h(x),y−x⟩ for all x,y. It is λ-strongly convex (λ>0) if it lies above tangent parabolas: h(y)≥h(x)+⟨∇h(x),y−x⟩+2λ​∥y−x∥2; for a C2 function this means ∇2h⪰λId. Example: h(x)=2L​∥x∥2 is L-strongly convex. Gradient descent xk+1​=xk​−τ∇h(xk​) is stable when ∇h is L-Lipschitz and τ<2/L.

Grönwall’s lemma. If E′(t)≤−cE(t) for t≥0, then E(t)≤E(0)e−ct. Proof: dtd​(ectE(t))=ect(E′+cE)≤0, so ectE(t) is non-increasing. Used in §1 and §7 (rates), §6 (Langevin). more · convexity

Refresher — push-forward and the continuity equation

The push-forward T#​α moves each bit of mass of α from x to T(x): ∫gd(T#​α)=∫g(T(x))dα(x); if X∼α then T(X)∼T#​α. Now let every point move along a velocity field: x˙(t)=vt​(x(t)), and let αt​ be the law of x(t) when x(0)∼α0​. Then αt​ solves the continuity equation

∂t​αt​+div(αt​vt​)=0,

which means, in weak form, dtd​∫φdαt​=∫⟨∇φ,vt​⟩dαt​ for all smooth test functions φ.

Why: ∫φdαt​=E[φ(x(t))] and dtd​φ(x(t))=⟨∇φ(x(t)),vt​(x(t))⟩ (chain rule). The strong form follows by one integration by parts. Mass is conserved: it is moved, never created. Particle (Lagrangian) and density (Eulerian) descriptions are the same object: the PDE for αt​ is equivalent to the ODE x˙=vt​(x) for its particles. Used everywhere from §2 on. This is the language of Lesson 6 (dynamic OT, Benamou–Brenier). more · push-forward

Refresher — W2​, Brenier maps, McCann interpolation, quantiles (Lessons 1–3)

W22​(α,β)=minπ∈U(α,β)​∫∥x−y∥2dπ. Brenier: if α has a density, the optimal plan is a map T=∇φ with φ convex, and W22​(α,β)=∫∥x−T(x)∥2dα. McCann interpolation: αs​=((1−s)Id+sT)#​α, s∈[0,1], is a constant-speed geodesic: W2​(αs​,αr​)=∣s−r∣W2​(α,β) (Lesson 3, §6). On the line: W22​(α,β)=∫01​∣Qα​(s)−Qβ​(s)∣2ds with the quantile functions Q=C−1 (Lesson 3 refresher). Gaussians: W22​(N(m,σ2),N(m′,σ′2))=(m−m′)2+(σ−σ′)2 on R, and ∥m−m′∥2+B(Σ,Σ′)2 in Rd (Lesson 3 refresher). Used in §2 (JKO), §3 (gradient of W22​), §7 (geodesic convexity), §9 (Gaussians). more

Refresher — Kantorovich potentials for the quadratic cost (Lesson 4)

For the cost c(x,y)=21​∥x−y∥2, duality reads 21​W22​(α,β)=maxφ(x)+ψ(y)≤c(x,y)​∫φdα+∫ψdβ. At the optimum, 21​∥x∥2−φ(x)=u(x) is convex and its gradient is the Brenier map: T=∇u=Id−∇φ, i.e. ∇φ(x)=x−T(x). Used in §3 (the first variation of 21​W22​(⋅,β) is φ) and in Exercise 6 of the sheet. more

Refresher — divergence, Laplacian, integration by parts

For a vector field w=(w1​,…,wd​), divw=∑i​∂i​wi​; the Laplacian is Δg=div(∇g)=∑i​∂i2​g. Integration by parts (no boundary term when w or φ decays fast enough, or is compactly supported):

∫φdivwdx=−∫⟨∇φ,w⟩dx.

Two identities used again and again: div(ρ∇logρ)=div(∇ρ)=Δρ (because ρ∇logρ=∇ρ), and div(ρ∇g)=⟨∇ρ,∇g⟩+ρΔg. Used in §3 (Proposition 15.7), §4 (heat and Fokker–Planck), §6 (Langevin). more

Refresher — entropy, KL, Fisher information, with Gaussian formulas

For α=ρdx, the neg-entropy is ∫ρlogρdx (minus the Shannon entropy; it is small for spread-out densities). The relative entropy is KL(α∣β)=∫logdβdα​dα≥0 (Jensen), with equality iff α=β. The relative Fisher information is I(α∣β)=∫​∇logdβdα​​2dα. Gaussian formulas on R (all used below):

∫ρlogρ=−logσ−21​log(2πe)for N(m,σ2),
KL(N(m,s2)∣N(0,1))=21​(s2+m2−1−logs2),I(N(m,s2)∣N(0,1))=m2+(s−s1​)2.

(For the last one: ∇logρβ​ρ​(x)=−s2x−m​+x; with x=m+sZ this is m+(s−s1​)Z, whose mean square is m2+(s−s1​)2.) more · f-divergences

Refresher — Brownian motion and stochastic differential equations, just what is needed

A standard Brownian motion Bt​ in Rd starts at 0, has independent increments, and Bt​−Bs​∼N(0,(t−s)Id). The SDE dXt​=b(Xt​)dt+2​dBt​ means Xt​=X0​+∫0t​b(Xs​)ds+2​Bt​; it is simulated by the Euler–Maruyama scheme Xk+1​=Xk​+hb(Xk​)+2h​ξk​ with independent ξk​∼N(0,Id). The one fact behind every computation of §6: over a short time h, the noise moves the point by O(h​) (much more than the drift, O(h)), and its second-order effect is deterministic: E[⟨∇2φ2​Bh​,2​Bh​⟩]=2hΔφ. The law αt​ of Xt​ then solves the Fokker–Planck equation ∂t​αt​=−div(αt​b)+Δαt​. more · Fokker–Planck

Refresher — kernels and the maximum mean discrepancy

A symmetric kernel k is positive definite if ∑i,j​ci​cj​k(xi​,xj​)≥0 for all points and coefficients. The MMD between two measures is MMDk2​(α,β)=∬kd(α−β)d(α−β)=∬kdαdα−2∬kdαdβ+∬kdβdβ. Examples: the Gaussian kernel e−∥x−y∥2/(2σ2) and the energy-distance kernel k(x,y)=−∥x−y∥, which is only conditionally positive definite (non-negative on zero-mass signed measures), enough to make MMD2≥0. MMD is defined for any measures, including point clouds. Used in §5 and §8. more

Notation decoder#

The resources use slightly different notation, and three of their conventions change the clock of a flow by a factor 2 (see the last rows). This page follows the book (OT4ML), except for the Wasserstein gradient, written ∇W​ as on the exercise sheet.

SymbolReadMeaning, and other notations in the resources
P2​(Rd)“measures with finite second moment”Probability measures with ∫∥x∥2dα<∞; the space where W2​ is finite (the sheet writes W2​(Rd)).
α, αt​, ρ, ρt​“the measure, at time t; its density”α=ρdx when α has a density. StatOT writes μ, and often identifies μ with its density.
f(α)“the energy”A function of a measure, to be minimised (entropy, KL, MMD, risk of a network). The syllabus and many papers write F(ρ), CompOT F(α), StatOT F(μ).
τ, α(ℓ)“step size”, “ℓ-th JKO iterate”JKO time step; α(ℓ) approximates αt​ at t=ℓτ.
δαδf​(α)(x)“first variation of f at α”A function of x, defined up to a constant (§3). OT4ML writes δf(α), CompOT F′(α), StatOT δF(μ).
∇W​f(α)“Wasserstein gradient”The vector field ∇x​δαδf​(α) (§3). The sheet writes ∇W​f; OT4ML and StatOT use a double-struck nabla.
div, Δ“divergence”, “Laplacian”See the refresher above.
V, β=Z−1e−Vdx“potential”, “Gibbs measure”β is the target of the Fokker–Planck flow (StatOT calls it π). In §11, V is also the value matrix of attention.
H, W, I“entropy, distance, Fisher information”In §7: H=KL(α∣β), W=W2​(α,β), I=I(α∣β).
λ, κ“convexity constant”, “PL constant”λ-geodesic convexity; Polyak–Łojasiewicz inequality with constant κ (§7).
n, X=(x1​,…,xn​), F(X)“particles”F(X)=f(n1​∑i​δxi​​): the energy seen as a function of the positions (§5).
k(x,y), W(x−y)“interaction kernel”Energies ∬kdαdα (OT4ML) or 21​∬W(x−y)dαdα (StatOT): the factor 21​ removes a factor 2 from the gradient.
Bt​, h“Brownian motion”, “time step”Langevin dynamics and its Euler–Maruyama discretisation (§6).
N(m,Σ), B“Gaussian”, “Bures”Gaussian closures (§9); on R the Gaussians are the half-plane of pairs (m,σ).

clock conventions“factors of 2”(1) CompOT’s step argminW22​+τF is a JKO step of size τ/2. (2) ∬kdαdα has gradient 2∫∇x​k, 21​∬W has ∫∇W. (3) Gradient descent on positions, x˙i​=−∇xi​​F, runs the Wasserstein flow n times slower. Same paths, different speeds.

Colour code of the figures: initial measure α0​ (orange-red), target or limit measure β (blue), the flow αt​, its particles and its velocity field (green), a second scheme to compare with (JKO iterates, Langevin particles, explicit steps — purple); mixtures and reference curves are grey.

1. The model: gradient flows in Rd OT4ML p. 356 · CompOT p. 153#

The gradient flow x˙=−∇h(x) can be discretised explicitly (gradient descent: take the slope where you stand) or implicitly (take the slope where you land, by solving a small minimisation problem); the implicit step only needs a distance, which is why it is the one that will move measures.

Why start with points#

The whole lesson answers one question: how do you run gradient descent when the unknown is a probability measure? Machine learning is full of such problems: fit a cloud of generated samples to a data set (minimise an MMD), sample a Bayesian posterior (minimise a KL divergence), train a wide neural network (minimise a risk that depends on the distribution of its neurons). For a vector x∈Rd the answer is gradient descent, x−τ∇h(x). For a measure α the same formula breaks down: “α−τg” is a signed measure, whose mass can become negative. Before fixing this (§2), we look at the Euclidean scheme from the angle that will survive: a step is a minimisation problem that balances “decrease the energy” against “do not move too far”.

Explicit and implicit Euler steps#

In the course OT4ML §15.1, p. 356

Euclidean gradient flows. If we restrict (15.1) to finite dimensions and assume αt​=δx(t)​ and α=δx​ (single Dirac measures), this matches the implicit Euler scheme:

x(t+τ)∈xargmin​{2τ1​∥x−x(t)∥2+h(x)},

where h(x)=f(δx​). When h is differentiable and the minimizer is unique, the solution is characterized by the implicit Euler formula x(t+τ)=(Id+τ∇h)−1(x(t)). In contrast, the explicit Euler scheme is: x(t+τ)=(Id−τ∇h)(x(t))=x(t)−τ∇h(x(t)). Both schemes converge as τ→0 to:

x˙(t)=−∇h(x(t)).(15.2)
In the course CompOT (9.24)–(9.25), p. 153

[(9.24), gradient descent] corresponds to a so-called “explicit” minimization scheme and only applies for smooth functions F. For nonsmooth functions, one can use instead an “implicit” scheme, which is also called the proximal-point algorithm […] a(ℓ+1)=ProxτF∥⋅∥​(a(ℓ))=argmina​21​​a−a(ℓ)​2+τF(a). […] For convex F, iterations (9.25) always converge, for any value of τ>0.

(15.1)
The JKO step on measures, defined in §2. The book introduces the Euclidean schemes as its restriction to single Diracs; here we start from them.
h
The energy to minimise, a function on Rd (the book writes h(x)=f(δx​) because it will be the restriction to Diracs of an energy f on measures, §2).
τ
The time step: x(t+τ) approximates the exact flow at time t+τ.
2τ1​∥x−x(t)∥2
The price of moving from x(t) to x. A small τ makes moving expensive: small steps.
argmin{⋯}
The next point is the best compromise between the energy h(x) and the cost of moving there. “∈” because there may be several minimisers.
(Id+τ∇h)−1
The resolvent: x(t+τ) is the point x such that x+τ∇h(x)=x(t). It is an equation to solve, not a formula to evaluate.
ProxτF​
The proximal operator: the same minimisation, with CompOT’s normalisation (multiply the book’s objective by τ). Same minimiser.
(15.2)
The gradient flow: the curve that always goes in the direction of steepest descent, at speed ∥∇h∥.

Where the implicit formula comes from. If h is differentiable, the objective 2τ1​∥x−xk​∥2+h(x) has zero gradient at its minimiser xk+1​:

τxk+1​−xk​​+∇h(xk+1​)=0⟺xk+1​=xk​−τ∇h(xk+1​).

So the implicit step is a gradient step with the slope taken where you land; the explicit step takes it where you stand. Both are first-order approximations of (15.2): τxk+1​−xk​​≈x˙.

Worked example — a stiff quadratic, h(x)=2L​x2 with L=10, x0​=1

The exact flow is x˙=−Lx, so x(t)=e−Lt. Each scheme multiplies xk​ by a fixed factor:

  • explicit: xk+1​=xk​−τLxk​=(1−τL)xk​;
  • implicit: xk+1​+τLxk+1​=xk​, so xk+1​=1+τLxk​​.
step τexplicit factorimplicit factorx at t=1: explicitimplicitexact e−10
0.01 (100 steps)0.90.90912.66×10−57.26×10−54.54×10−5
0.25 (4 steps)−1.50.28575.066.66×10−34.54×10−5

With a small step both schemes are accurate (one undershoots, the other overshoots: first order). With τ=0.25>2/L the explicit factor has modulus 1.5>1: the iterates oscillate and blow up, (−1.5)4=5.06. The implicit factor 1/(1+τL) is in (0,1) for every τ>0: the iterates decrease towards the minimiser, whatever the step.

The implicit step does not need a gradient

For h(x)=∣x∣ on R (no derivative at 0), the implicit step is perfectly defined: minimising 2τ1​(x−y)2+∣x∣ gives the soft-thresholding x=sign(y)max(∣y∣−τ,0). With τ=0.3: y=0.7↦0.4, y=0.2↦0, y=−1↦−0.7. Small values are set exactly to zero — the mechanism behind sparsity in the Lasso. Keep this in mind: on measures, the entropy will play the role of a non-smooth energy (it is +∞ on point clouds), and the implicit step will handle it.

What a gradient flow guarantees: dissipation and rates#

Three facts about x˙=−∇h(x) will be lifted, one by one, to measures in §7. Their Euclidean proofs fit in a few lines.

In the course OT4ML §15.2, p. 373

Dissipation and finite metric length. […] For the classical gradient flow of a smooth function h:Rd→R, x˙t​=−∇h(xt​), the chain rule gives dtd​h(xt​)=−∥∇h(xt​)∥2=−∥x˙t​∥2.

Three facts (Euclidean model; the Wasserstein versions are OT4ML Prop. 15.26, Thm. 15.28 and Prop. 15.29, §7)
  1. Dissipation. dtd​h(xt​)=−∥∇h(xt​)∥2≤0: the energy decreases, at the rate of the squared slope.
  2. Convex case. If h is convex with a minimiser x⋆: h(xt​)−h(x⋆)≤2t∥x0​−x⋆∥2​.
  3. Strongly convex case. If h is λ-strongly convex, it satisfies the Polyak–Łojasiewicz (PL) inequality ∥∇h(x)∥2≥2λ(h(x)−h⋆), and then h(xt​)−h⋆≤e−2λt(h(x0​)−h⋆).
Idea of the proofs

(1) is the chain rule. (2): the distance to the minimiser decreases at a rate at least equal to the energy gap (convexity says the descent direction points towards x⋆); integrate. (3): PL turns the dissipation identity into a differential inequality E′≤−2λE; Grönwall.

Full proofs

(1) dtd​h(xt​)=⟨∇h(xt​),x˙t​⟩=⟨∇h(xt​),−∇h(xt​)⟩=−∥∇h(xt​)∥2.

(2)

  1. dtd​21​∥xt​−x⋆∥2=⟨xt​−x⋆,x˙t​⟩=−⟨∇h(xt​),xt​−x⋆⟩.
    Chain rule, and x˙t​=−∇h(xt​).
  2. −⟨∇h(xt​),xt​−x⋆⟩≤−(h(xt​)−h(x⋆)).
    Convexity at xt​, evaluated at y=x⋆: h(x⋆)≥h(xt​)+⟨∇h(xt​),x⋆−xt​⟩.
  3. ∫0t​(h(xs​)−h⋆)ds≤21​∥x0​−x⋆∥2−21​∥xt​−x⋆∥2≤21​∥x0​−x⋆∥2.
    Integrate lines 1–2 from 0 to t.
  4. t(h(xt​)−h⋆)≤∫0t​(h(xs​)−h⋆)ds≤21​∥x0​−x⋆∥2.
    s↦h(xs​) is non-increasing by (1), so every value on [0,t] is at least the last one. Divide by t.

(3)

  1. h⋆=ymin​h(y)≥ymin​(h(x)+⟨∇h(x),y−x⟩+2λ​∥y−x∥2)=h(x)−2λ∥∇h(x)∥2​.
    Strong convexity gives a lower bound by a parabola in y; its minimum is at y=x−∇h(x)/λ (complete the square). Rearranged: the PL inequality.
  2. With E(t)=h(xt​)−h⋆: E′(t)=−∥∇h(xt​)∥2≤−2λE(t).(1), then PL.
  3. E(t)≤e−2λtE(0).Grönwall (refresher).

For h=2L​x2: h(xt​)=2L​e−2Ltx02​, so (3) holds with equality and λ=L.

The implicit step as a “minimizing movement”#

Look at the implicit step once more: it only uses the energy and the squared distance. Nothing in it requires a vector space. On any metric space (X,d) one can define

x(ℓ+1)∈x∈Xargmin​ 2τ1​d(x(ℓ),x)2+h(x),

a minimizing movement. CompOT writes it explicitly (Remark 9.11, (9.31), p. 154, with d2+τF, the same minimiser for a step τ/2) and adds: “The implicit step is always stable, is also defined for nonsmooth F, but is usually not accessible in closed form” (p. 155). The general theory of the limits τ→0 in metric spaces is due to Ambrosio, Gigli and Savaré (OT4ML Defs. 15.8–15.9, p. 359). The plan of the lesson: take X=P2​(Rd) and d=W2​.

In machine learning — step sizes and proximal steps

Training a model by gradient descent is the explicit scheme applied to the loss h(θ) of its parameters θ: the learning rate is τ, and the worked example is the reason why a learning rate above 2/L (L the largest curvature of the loss) makes training diverge. Proximal steps are used when part of the objective is non-smooth: for the Lasso, minθ​21​∥y−Aθ∥2+μ∥θ∥1​, the proximal gradient method (ISTA) alternates a gradient step on the smooth part and a soft-thresholding on the ℓ1 part. StatOT (§6.2.2, (6.12)–(6.14), pp. 188–189) uses exactly this split to explain sampling algorithms: the potential energy is the smooth part, the entropy the non-smooth part, and “the proximal operator on the Wasserstein space” is the JKO step of §2.

Pitfall — “implicit” does not mean “free”

The implicit step is stable for every τ, but each step is an optimisation problem; it is cheap only when that problem has structure (a closed form, convexity, a sparse Hessian). On measures we will meet both cases: closed forms for Diracs and Gaussians (§2), a convex problem in one dimension (§2), and particle methods everywhere else (§5).

Reflexes
  • When you see argminx​2τ1​d(x,xk​)2+h(x) → an implicit Euler (proximal) step of the gradient flow of h for the distance d; first-order condition τxk+1​−xk​​=−∇h(xk+1​).
  • To prove a rate for a gradient flow → differentiate the energy (dissipation), then find an inequality between the slope and the energy gap (convexity, PL) and integrate.

For h(x)=21​x2 and x0​=2, compute one explicit and one implicit step with τ=0.5, and the exact flow at t=0.5.

Answer

Explicit: 2−0.5⋅2=1. Implicit: x+0.5x=2, so x=4/3≈1.333. Exact: 2e−0.5≈1.213, in between. We will meet these three numbers again in §2: they are the JKO step of a Dirac.

2. The JKO scheme: an implicit step in W2​ OT4ML Def. 15.1, p. 356#

A JKO step replaces the current measure by the best compromise between a lower energy and a small transport distance W2​; for a Dirac it is the Euclidean implicit step, for a Gaussian and the entropy it is one quadratic equation, and on the line it is a convex problem in the quantile function.

Why measure the step with W2​#

There are two natural ways to go from a measure α to a nearby one.

Mixing (“vertical”)

(1−ϑ)α+ϑβ: mass disappears here and reappears there, without travelling. It is the linear structure of measures.

Moving (“horizontal”)

(Id+τv)#​α: every bit of mass slides from x to x+τv(x). It is the transport structure, measured by W2​: W22​(α,(Id+τv)#​α)≤τ2∫∥v∥2dα.

The energies of this lesson are decreased by moving mass: spreading a density (entropy), pulling samples towards data (MMD), sliding neurons towards useful features (§10). And W2​ heavily penalises mixing: from α=δ0​ to (1−ϑ)δ0​+ϑδ1​ the distance is ϑ​ (mass ϑ must travel a distance 1), which is 0.1 for ϑ=0.01 — far more than the size ϑ of the change of weights. Measuring steps with W2​ therefore forces each step to be a small transport. (This is the phenomenon of Lesson 3, §6: the mixture path is infinitely long for W2​.)

The JKO step#

In the course OT4ML Def. 15.1, p. 356

Definition 15.1 (JKO minimizing movement). Given τ>0 and α(0), define recursively

α(ℓ+1)∈α∈P2​(Rd)argmin​{2τ1​W2​(α(ℓ),α)2+f(α)}.(15.1)

The piecewise-constant interpolation ατ​(t)=α(ℓ) for t∈[ℓτ,(ℓ+1)τ) is called a minimizing movement.

f(α)
The energy on measures that we want to decrease: an entropy, a KL divergence, an MMD to data… It may take the value +∞ (the entropy of a point cloud).
α(ℓ)
The current measure, after ℓ steps; it approximates the flow at time t=ℓτ.
2τ1​W2​(α(ℓ),α)2
The price of moving from α(ℓ) to α: the cheapest way to move the mass, in squared distance, divided by 2τ.
argmin
Exactly the implicit Euler step of §1, with ∥x−y∥ replaced by W2​. When f is convex along W2​ geodesics (§7) and τ is small, the minimiser exists and is unique; we use this freely.
ατ​(t)
The staircase curve “stay at α(ℓ) during [ℓτ,(ℓ+1)τ)”. As τ→0 it converges (under assumptions) to a curve αt​, the Wasserstein gradient flow of f (§4).
JKO
Jordan, Kinderlehrer and Otto (1998), who introduced the scheme to show that the Fokker–Planck equation is the gradient flow of the free energy for W2​ (cited in CompOT p. 154 and StatOT p. 183).
Same step, three normalisations
  • OT4ML (above): 2τ1​W22​+f — the step has length τ in time.
  • StatOT (6.14), p. 189: proxhH​(μ)=argminν​{hH(ν)+21​W22​(μ,ν)}, “the proximal operator on the Wasserstein space” — the same step with τ=h (multiply OT4ML’s objective by τ).
  • CompOT Remark 9.10, (9.27), p. 153: argminα​W2​(α,α(ℓ))2+τF(α) with “the time t=τℓ”. Dividing by τ gives 2(τ/2)1​W22​+F: a JKO step of size τ/2, so the iterates follow the flow at time τℓ/2. See the note on the sources below.

First example: one Dirac and a potential energy#

Take f(α)=∫Vdα (a potential energy: each bit of mass pays V where it sits) and start from a single Dirac α(ℓ)=δx​.

  1. W22​(δx​,α)=∫∥x−y∥2dα(y).
    The only coupling of δx​ and α sends all of α’s mass from x: it is δx​⊗α.
  2. 2τ1​W22​(δx​,α)+f(α)=∫(2τ∥y−x∥2​+V(y))dα(y).
    Both terms are integrals against α.
  3. The minimiser is δy⋆​ with y⋆∈argminy​2τ∥y−x∥2​+V(y).The average of a function against a probability measure is at least its minimum, with equality when all the mass sits at a minimiser.

So from a Dirac, the JKO step is exactly the Euclidean implicit step of h=V (this is the remark “restrict to α=δx​” of OT4ML p. 356). With V(y)=21​y2, x=2 and τ=0.5: y⋆=1+τx​=34​≈1.333, while the exact flow x˙=−x gives 2e−0.5≈1.213 and the explicit step gives 1 — the numbers of the quick check of §1. The mass does not spread: a potential energy moves each particle on its own (§4).

Second example: the heat equation, one Gaussian step by hand#

Now take the neg-entropy f(α)=∫ρlogρdx (and +∞ if α has no density). It is small for spread-out densities, so its gradient flow should spread mass: we will see in §4 that it is the heat equation ∂t​ρ=Δρ, whose solution from N(m,s2) is N(m,s2+2t). Let us run one JKO step from a Gaussian, on the line.

Proposition (JKO step of the entropy from a Gaussian; computed here)

On R, the JKO step (15.1) for f(α)=∫ρlogρ from α(ℓ)=N(m,σℓ2​) is α(ℓ+1)=N(m,σℓ+12​) with

σℓ+1​=2σℓ​+σℓ2​+4τ​​(the positive root of σ2−σℓ​σ−τ=0).
Idea

The minimiser is a Gaussian, and on Gaussians both terms are explicit: W22​ is the squared Euclidean distance between the pairs (m,σ), and the neg-entropy is −logσ plus a constant. One derivative in σ finishes the job.

Full derivation
  1. The minimiser is a Gaussian.Replacing a candidate α by the Gaussian Gauss(α) with the same mean and variance does not increase W22​(α(ℓ),⋅) (Gelbrich’s theorem, OT4ML Thm. 16.30, p. 439: equality between Gaussians, inequality in general) and does not increase the neg-entropy (the Gaussian has the largest entropy at given variance). This is the “Gaussian-preservation criterion” of OT4ML Thm. 16.31, p. 439. With a unique minimiser, it is Gaussian.
  2. ​2τ1​W22​(N(m,σℓ2​),N(m′,σ2))+f(N(m′,σ2))=2τ(m′−m)2+(σ−σℓ​)2​−logσ−21​log(2πe).​
    The 1D Gaussian formula W22​=(m−m′)2+(σ−σ′)2 (refresher) and ∫ρlogρ=−logσ−21​log(2πe) (refresher).
  3. m′=m: the mean does not move.Only the first term depends on m′.
  4. τσ−σℓ​​−σ1​=0⟺σ2−σℓ​σ−τ=0.
    Derivative in σ; the function of σ is strictly convex on (0,∞) (a parabola plus −log), so the zero of the derivative is the minimiser.
  5. σℓ+1​=21​(σℓ​+σℓ2​+4τ​)=σℓ​+σℓ​τ​+O(τ2).
    Positive root. Expanding σ2+4τ​=σ(1+σ22τ​−σ42τ2​+…).
  6. τσℓ+1​−σℓ​​→σ1​, i.e. dtd​σ2=2: the limit is σ(t)2=σ02​+2t, the heat flow.dtd​σ2=2σσ˙=2. Consistency of the scheme with the exact solution.
Worked example — σ0​=0.5, τ=0.25, four steps
time t=ℓτ0.250.50.751
JKO σℓ​0.80901.04761.24801.4236
exact 0.25+2t​0.86601.11801.32291.5
error =W2​ between the two0.05700.07040.07490.0764

First step: σ1​=21​(0.5+0.25+1​)=21​(0.5+1.1180)=0.8090. Halving the step halves the error at t=1: 0.0764, 0.0414, 0.0217, 0.0111 for τ=0.25, 0.125, 0.0625, 0.03125 — a first-order scheme, like the implicit Euler step. The implicit step underestimates the spreading (as the implicit step of §1 underestimated the decay). Independent check: the particle solver of the next subsection, with 400 particles, gives σ≈0.8092 after the first step.

Do the same computation for the Fokker–Planck energy f(α)=KL(α∣N(0,1))=∫ρlogρ+∫2x2​dα+const, from N(2,0.52) with τ=0.25.

Answer

On N(m′,σ2) the potential term is 21​(m′2+σ2). Mean: τm′−m​+m′=0, so m′=1+τm​=1.6. Standard deviation: τσ−σℓ​​+σ−σ1​=0, i.e. (1+τ)σ2−σℓ​σ−τ=0, so σ=2(1+τ)σℓ​+σℓ2​+4τ(1+τ)​​=2.50.5+1.5​​=0.6899. The exact flow (§4) is at (2e−0.25,1−0.75e−0.5​)=(1.5576,0.7383).

On the line: a convex problem in the quantile function#

For non-Gaussian data there is no closed form, but in one dimension the JKO step becomes a convex problem once the measure is described by its quantile function Q=C−1 (Lesson 3 refresher).

  1. W22​(α,α(ℓ))=∫01​(Q(s)−Qℓ​(s))2ds.
    The 1D formula: the optimal plan matches quantiles.
  2. ρ(Q(s))Q′(s)=1(0<s<1).
    Differentiate C(Q(s))=s: C′=ρ. Mass ds between the levels s and s+ds is spread over a length Q′(s)ds.
  3. ∫ρlogρdx=∫01​logρ(Q(s))ds=−∫01​logQ′(s)ds.
    Change of variables x=Q(s), dx=Q′(s)ds, and ρ(Q)Q′=1; then line 2 again.
  4. Qmin​ ∫01​(2τ(Q−Qℓ​)2​−logQ′)ds.
    The JKO step written in Q. It is strictly convex: Q↦Q′ is linear and −log is convex; the constraint “Q increasing” is enforced by the logarithm.

Particles. Put N particles x1​<⋯<xN​ at the levels sj​=(j−21​)/N, each carrying mass N1​, and give each gap the density xi+1​−xi​1/N​. Multiplying the discretised objective by N, a JKO step minimises

G(x)=i=1∑N​2τ(xi​−xi(ℓ)​)2​−i=1∑N−1​log(xi+1​−xi​)(+i∑​V(xi​) for Fokker–Planck).

Its optimality condition, τxi​−xi(ℓ)​​=xi​−xi−1​1​−xi+1​−xi​1​, is the implicit Euler step of the particle system x˙i​=xi​−xi−1​1​−xi+1​−xi​1​: a particle is pushed away from the side where its neighbour is closer, i.e. away from high density — diffusion seen from the particles. The Hessian of G is tridiagonal, so each Newton iteration costs O(N), and the step is solved for any τ.

Interactive figure (needs JavaScript).

What to look at: 160 particles start at the quantiles of a two-bump law (orange-red, dashed). Top: the exact flow at time t (green) and the JKO iterate at the last step before t (purple). Bottom: the motion of a few quantiles — exact curves (green) and JKO iterates (purple dots), a Lagrangian picture of the flow. Change the step τ: at t=1, the W2​ error of the JKO iterates is 0.0537, 0.0291, 0.0150, 0.0074 for τ=0.2, 0.1, 0.05, 0.025 (the distance travelled by the heat flow is 0.875): first order again. The last line of the readout runs the explicit scheme on the same particles: the smallest gap is 0.0065, so it is only stable for τ≲21​⋅0.00652≈2×10−5; with τ=0.01 the particles cross after 3 steps. Switch to Fokker–Planck: the mass drifts to the blue target and the errors are smaller (0.016 at τ=0.2).

In machine learning — proximal steps on distributions

Sampling. To sample a posterior β∝e−V, StatOT (§6.2.2, pp. 188–190) writes KL(⋅∣β)=∫Vdα+∫ρlogρ+const as “smooth + non-smooth” and proposes the proximal gradient algorithm on the Wasserstein space: a gradient step on the potential, then the JKO step (6.14) of the entropy. It converges fast but the JKO step is intractable in high dimension; the proximal sampler (StatOT §6.2.3, pp. 190–191) is an implementable cousin whose rates “exactly replicate the rates for the proximal point method from convex optimization”. Grids. On images or volumes, an entropic JKO step — W22​ replaced by its entropic version of Lesson 7 — is solved by generalised Sinkhorn iterations: “An entropic JKO step fixes the first marginal to the previous iterate and puts the energy on the second marginal” (OT4ML §8.6, p. 155, and Prop. 8.26).

Note on the sources — CompOT’s clock

CompOT Remark 9.10 (p. 153) uses the step argminα​W22​(α,α(ℓ))+τF(α) and says that α(ℓ) approximates the flow at “the time t=τℓ”. For p=2 this step is the JKO step of size τ/2, so the right time is τℓ/2. Check on one Dirac with F(α)=∫2x2​dα: the step is x↦x/(1+τ/2); with τ=0.01 and 100 steps, x100​/x0​=1.005−100=0.6073, close to e−1/2=0.6065 and far from e−1=0.3679. The limit PDE (9.28) is right; only the clock is off by a factor 2.

Reflexes
  • JKO step from a Dirac and a potential energy → the Euclidean implicit step, and the mass stays a Dirac.
  • JKO step with Gaussian data → restrict to Gaussians (when Gaussians are preserved) and minimise over (m,σ): W22​ is Euclidean in (m,σ) on the line.
  • JKO step on the line → write it in quantiles: W22​=∫(Q−Qℓ​)2, entropy =−∫logQ′.
  • Compare normalisations before comparing clocks: 2τ1​W22​+f (step τ) versus W22​+τF (step τ/2).

3. First variation and Wasserstein gradient OT4ML pp. 356–359#

Perturbing a measure by mixing gives the first variation δαδf​, a function (the value of adding a bit of mass at x); perturbing it by moving gives the Wasserstein gradient ∇W​f=∇δαδf​, a vector field (the direction in which moving mass increases f fastest).

Two ways to differentiate a function of a measure#

For h:Rd→R, the derivative answers “how does h change when x moves a little?”. For f(α) there are two ways to change α a little, the two moves of §2, and they give two derivatives:

The first variation#

In the course OT4ML Def. 15.2, pp. 356–357

Definition 15.2 (First variation). Assume that f(α)<+∞. A measurable function δf(α) is a first variation of f at α if, for every β∈P(Rd) such that δf(α) is integrable with respect to ∣β−α∣ and the mixture αϑ​ remains in the domain of f for small ϑ>0,

f(αϑ​)=f(α)+ϑ∫Rd​[δf(α)](x)d(β−α)(x)+o(ϑ)(ϑ↓0).

Because β−α has zero mass, δf(α) is determined only up to an additive constant.

αϑ​
The mixture (1−ϑ)α+ϑβ (defined just before, p. 356): remove a fraction ϑ of α everywhere and put it where β is.
δf(α)
A function of x∈Rd (the sheet writes δαδf​(α)(x)). Read δf(α)(x) as “the marginal value of a unit of mass placed at x”: adding mass where δf(α) is large increases f.
∫δf(α)d(β−α)
The directional derivative of f at α in the direction β−α. In Rd the analogue is h(x+ϑu)=h(x)+ϑ⟨∇h(x),u⟩+o(ϑ): δf(α) plays the role of ∇h(x) and the integral plays the role of the inner product.
“up to a constant”
Since ∫cd(β−α)=c−c=0, adding a constant to δf(α) changes nothing. Only differences of values, or the gradient ∇δf(α), are meaningful.

How to compute it. Write αϑ​=α+ϑη with η=β−α (zero mass), expand f(α+ϑη) to first order in ϑ, and read the coefficient of ϑ as ∫(⋯)dη. Four examples, each one line:

  1. Potential energy f(α)=∫Vdα: f(α+ϑη)=f(α)+ϑ∫Vdη exactly. So δαδf​=V.f is linear in α; its derivative is itself (OT4ML Ex. 15.11, p. 360).
  2. Interaction energy f(α)=∬k(x,y)dα(x)dα(y), k symmetric: f(α+ϑη)=f(α)+2ϑ∬k(x,y)dα(y)dη(x)+ϑ2∬kdηdη. So δαδf​(x)=2∫k(x,y)dα(y).Expand the product (α+ϑη)⊗(α+ϑη); the two cross terms are equal because k is symmetric (OT4ML (15.9), p. 361).
  3. Neg-entropy f(α)=∫ρlogρ, with η of density ζ: dϑd​[(ρ+ϑζ)log(ρ+ϑζ)]ϑ=0​=ζ(logρ+1). So δαδf​=logρ+1.Derivative of slogs is logs+1; differentiate under the integral (OT4ML Ex. 15.13, p. 361). The constant 1 can be dropped.
  4. Relative entropy f(α)=KL(α∣β) with β=Z−1e−Vdx: KL(α∣β)=∫ρlogρ+∫Vdα+logZ, so δαδf​=logρ+V+1=logρβ​ρ​+const.Sum of lines 1 and 3; logρβ​=−V−logZ.
Worked example — three points and the variance

Let f(α)=41​∬(x−y)2dα(x)dα(y) on R. Expanding the square, f(α)=21​Var(α). By line 2 with k=41​(x−y)2:

δαδf​(x)=21​∫(x−y)2dα(y)=21​(x−m)2+21​Var(α),m=∫ydα(y).

Take α=31​(δ0​+δ1​+δ5​): m=2, Var=34+1+9​=314​, f(α)=37​. Mix towards β=δ3​. The definition predicts

dϑd​f(αϑ​)​0​=∫21​(x−m)2d(δ3​−α)=21​(3−2)2−21​Var(α)=21​−37​=−611​≈−1.8333.

Numerically, (f(αϑ​)−f(α))/ϑ=−1.83338 for ϑ=10−5. ✓ Adding mass at 3, close to the mean, lowers the variance: δαδf​(3)=21​+37​ is below the average value ∫δαδf​dα=37​+37​.

The Wasserstein gradient#

In the course OT4ML Def. 15.5, (15.4), p. 358

Definition 15.5 (Wasserstein gradient). Assume that f admits a smooth first variation δf(α). In the smooth formal calculus on P2​(Rd), the Wasserstein gradient of f at α is the gradient vector field ∇W​f(α)=∇x​δf(α). […] The associated formal gradient flow is the continuity equation

∂t∂αt​​+div(−∇W​f(αt​)αt​)=0.(15.4)
In the course OT4ML Prop. 15.7, p. 358

Proposition 15.7 (Formal Wasserstein gradient). Assume that f admits a smooth first variation δf(α) and that α has a smooth positive density. Let v be a sufficiently regular velocity field, compactly supported or satisfying a no-flux boundary condition. For perturbations generated by (Id+τv)#​α, the differential of f is

dτd​​τ=0​f((Id+τv)#​α)=∫⟨∇δf(α)(x),v(x)⟩dα(x).

Hence, for the Riemannian metric ∥v∥L2(α)2​=∫∥v∥2dα, the Wasserstein gradient is the vector field ∇W​f(α)=∇δf(α).

∇x​δf(α)
The ordinary gradient, in x, of the function δf(α): a vector field on Rd. The additive constant disappears. (OT4ML and StatOT write it with a double-struck nabla; the sheet writes ∇W​f.)
(Id+τv)#​α
Move every bit of mass from x to x+τv(x): a horizontal perturbation in the direction v.
∥v∥L2(α)2​
The size of a velocity field, weighted by the mass that moves: the kinetic energy of the motion. It is the metric hidden in W2​: W22​(α,(Id+τv)#​α)=τ2∥v∥L2(α)2​ when the displacement is optimal (OT4ML p. 359; StatOT §5.3).
“Riemannian gradient”
The derivative in the direction v is the inner product ⟨∇W​f,v⟩L2(α)​: exactly how ⟨∇h(x),u⟩ represents Dh(x)[u] in Rd. Among unit velocities, ⟨∇W​f,v⟩L2(α)​ is most negative for v=−∇W​f/∥∇W​f∥ (Cauchy–Schwarz): −∇W​f is the direction of steepest descent.
(15.4)
The gradient flow: every bit of mass moves with velocity −∇W​f(αt​) at its current position; the continuity equation (refresher) turns this into a PDE for αt​. §4 derives it from the JKO step.
Idea of the proof

Moving mass by τv is, to first order, the zero-mass perturbation −τdiv(αv) (mass leaves where v diverges). Plug it into the first variation, then integrate by parts to move the derivative from αv to δf(α).

Full proof (formal, as in the book)
  1. ∫ψd((Id+τv)#​α)=∫ψ(x+τv(x))dα(x)=∫ψdα+τ∫⟨∇ψ,v⟩dα+o(τ)
    Definition of the push-forward, then a first-order Taylor expansion of the test function ψ.
  2. τ∫⟨∇ψ,v⟩ρdx=−τ∫ψdiv(ρv)dx.
    Integration by parts (refresher); no boundary term because v is compactly supported.
  3. So, as measures (tested against every ψ): (Id+τv)#​α=α−τdiv(αv)+o(τ).Lines 1–2. The perturbation −τdiv(αv) has zero mass: ∫div(αv)=0.
  4. f((Id+τv)#​α)=f(α)−τ∫δf(α)div(αv)dx+o(τ).
    First variation applied to the zero-mass perturbation of line 3 (formal: Definition 15.2 is stated for mixtures; the smooth calculus extends it to such perturbations).
  5. −∫δf(α)div(αv)dx=∫⟨∇δf(α),v⟩dα.
    Integration by parts again, now with φ=δf(α) and w=αv.
  6. The derivative is the L2(α) inner product of v with ∇δf(α), which is therefore the Riesz representative — the gradient for that metric. □Lines 4–5. This is OT4ML’s proof, p. 358–359; StatOT Prop. 5.10 (p. 152) does the same along a curve μt​.
Worked example, continued — the gradient pulls points to the mean

For f=21​Var: ∇W​f(α)(x)=dxd​21​(x−m)2=x−m. On α=31​(δ0​+δ1​+δ5​) it equals (−2,−1,3) at the three points: the descent velocities −∇W​f=(2,1,−3) pull every point towards the mean m=2. Check of Proposition 15.7 with the dilation v(x)=x: the prediction is ∫(x−m)xdα=Var(α)=314​≈4.6667; numerically τ1​(f((1+τ)Id#​α)−f(α))=4.666669 for τ=10−6. ✓ (Indeed f of a dilation by 1+τ is (1+τ)2f, whose derivative is 2f=314​.)

The table of Wasserstein gradients#

Combining the four computations above with the definition gives the gradients of all the energies of this lesson. The last column says what the mass does along the flow x˙=−∇W​f(α)(x).

energy f(α)first variation δαδf​Wasserstein gradient ∇W​falong the flow, mass at x…
potential ∫VdαV∇Vslides down V, ignoring the rest
neg-entropy ∫ρlogρlogρ+1∇logρ (the score)leaves high density (diffusion)
internal energy ∫g(ρ)g′(ρ)g′′(ρ)∇ρnonlinear diffusion

Sources: OT4ML Ex. 15.11, Ex. 15.13, (15.9) and p. 362 (pp. 360–362); StatOT Examples 5.11–5.13 (pp. 152–153), which use 21​∬W(x−y) and get no factor 2; StatOT (5.30) (p. 170) for W22​; exercise sheet, Exercises 1, 4 and 6.

The gradient of 21​W22​, and the barycenter algorithm of Lesson 3#

The last row of the table deserves a derivation: it connects this lesson to Lesson 3, §9.

  1. 21​W22​(α,β)=φ(x)+ψ(y)≤21​∥x−y∥2max​ ∫φdα+∫ψdβ.
    Kantorovich duality for the cost 21​∥x−y∥2 (refresher).
  2. δαδ​(21​W22​(⋅,β))(α)=φα​(an optimal potential).
    “Envelope theorem”: the derivative of a maximum of functions that are linear in α is the derivative of the maximised one, ∫φα​dη (formal; this is the solution of Exercise 6 of the sheet, §13).
  3. ∇W​(21​W22​(⋅,β))(α)=∇φα​=Id−T,
    where T is the Brenier map from α to β.For the quadratic cost, 21​∥x∥2−φα​ is convex with gradient T (Lesson 4).
  4. An explicit gradient step of size τ moves x to x−τ(x−T(x))=(1−τ)x+τT(x): it lands on the McCann geodesic from α to β, at the fraction τ.Push α by Id−τ∇W​f. With τ=1 it lands on β in one step.

Now take the barycenter energy of Lesson 3, F(α)=∑k​λk​21​W22​(α,βk​). By linearity, ∇W​F(α)=∑k​λk​(Id−Tk​)=Id−∑k​λk​Tk​, where Tk​ is the Brenier map from α to βk​. A gradient step of size 1 is

α ⟼ (Id−∇W​F(α))#​α=(k∑​λk​Tk​)#​α,

which is exactly the fixed-point algorithm of Lesson 3 (“average the optimal maps, push the measure”). Its descent inequality (F decreases by at least W22​ of the step, Lesson 3) is the descent property of a gradient step, and its fixed points, ∑k​λk​Tk​=Id, are the zeros of the Wasserstein gradient. This is the interpretation of Zemel and Panaretos (2019) quoted in Lesson 3. Example: for β1​=N(0,1), β2​=N(4,9), λ=(21​,21​), from any N(m,σ2) the averaged map is x↦2+σ2​(x−m), and one step lands on the barycenter N(2,4).

In machine learning — the Wasserstein gradient is the training signal of a generator

A generative model produces samples x=Gθ​(z) from noise z∼ζ; its law is αθ​=(Gθ​)#​ζ. To train it, one minimises a loss of the generated distribution, f(αθ​), for instance MMD2(αθ​,βdata​) or a Sinkhorn divergence (Lesson 7). Changing θ in a direction u moves each sample by ∂θ​Gθ​(z)u, so Proposition 15.7 (with this displacement field) gives the chain rule

∇θ​f(αθ​)=∫(∂θ​Gθ​(z))⊤∇W​f(αθ​)(Gθ​(z))dζ(z).

In words: the Wasserstein gradient tells each generated sample where to move, and backpropagation pulls these per-sample directions back to the parameters. With the MMD loss, the direction at a sample x is 2∫∇x​k(x,y)d(αθ​−β)(y): away from the other generated samples, towards the data. This is what automatic differentiation computes when a loss is written as a function of a minibatch of generated samples (with the factor n of §5). Generators trained this way with an MMD loss were proposed by Dziugaite, Roy and Ghahramani (2015), with Sinkhorn losses by Genevay, Peyré and Cuturi (2018) (both cited in OT4ML).

Pitfall — a function is not a vector field

δαδf​ is a scalar function defined up to a constant; ∇W​f is a vector field. The flow is driven by the gradient of the first variation: a first variation that is constant on the support of α produces no motion at all, even if it is very large. This is what happens at a stationary point (§10).

Pitfall — the factor 2 of interaction energies

∬kdαdα has first variation 2∫k(⋅,y)dα(y), not ∫k(⋅,y)dα(y): α appears twice. StatOT puts a 21​ in front (21​∬W(x−y)) precisely to remove it. Missing this factor does not change the trajectories, only the clock.

Reflexes
  • To compute ∇W​f: replace α by α+ϑη, keep the term in ϑ, write it ∫(⋯)dη, take the gradient in x of (⋯).
  • Entropy → the score ∇logρ; potential → ∇V; interaction → a kernel average of ∇k; 21​W22​(⋅,β) → Id−T.
  • A sum of energies → a sum of gradients (KL = potential + entropy).

Compute δαδf​ and ∇W​f for f(α)=(∫xdα)2 on R (the squared mean). What does the flow do?

Answer

With m=∫xdα: f(α+ϑη)=(m+ϑ∫xdη)2=m2+2ϑm∫xdη+O(ϑ2), so δαδf​(x)=2mx and ∇W​f=2m, the same vector at every point. The flow translates the whole measure rigidly with velocity −2m: m˙=−2m, m(t)=m0​e−2t, and the shape never changes. (This is Exercise 4 (1) of the sheet with A=1.)

4. The limit PDE: one equation, four classical flows OT4ML pp. 358–364#

As τ→0, each JKO step moves the mass with velocity −∇δαδf​, so the steps converge to the continuity equation ∂t​αt​=div(αt​∇δαδf​(αt​)); with a potential it is transport by −∇V, with the entropy the heat equation, with an interaction an aggregation equation, with a KL to e−V the Fokker–Planck equation — and the energy always decreases at the rate ∫​∇δαδf​​2dαt​.

From the JKO step to the velocity field#

In the course OT4ML §15.1, p. 359

From the JKO step to the velocity field. A first-order expansion of the JKO step explains why (15.4) uses the vector field ∇W​f(α). This is a formal local argument: assume that αt​ is absolutely continuous and that, for the nearby competitors selected by the JKO step, the optimal map from αt​ can be written as Id+τv. For these optimal displacement representatives, W22​(αt​,(Id+τv)#​αt​)=τ2∥v∥L2(αt​)2​. The local JKO objective therefore reads

vmin​ 2τ​∥v∥L2(αt​)2​+f((Id+τv)#​αt​),

[…] The two expansions […] give the first-order problem

vmin​ f(αt​)+τ∫[21​∥v(x)∥2+⟨∇W​f(αt​)(x),v(x)⟩]dαt​(x)+o(τ).

Its pointwise minimizer is v=−∇W​f(αt​), which gives the velocity in the continuity equation.

competitors (Id+τv)#​αt​
Near αt​, look for the next step among the measures obtained by moving the mass by τv; the unknown is now a velocity field v.
2τ​∥v∥L2(αt​)2​
The JKO price 2τ1​W22​ of that move, 2τ1​⋅τ2∥v∥L22​.
“the two expansions”
(Id+τv)#​αt​=αt​−τdiv(vαt​)+o(τ) and f((Id+τv)#​αt​)=f(αt​)+τ∫⟨∇W​f,v⟩dαt​+o(τ): Proposition 15.7 (§3).
“pointwise minimizer”
The integrand 21​∥v∥2+⟨g,v⟩ is minimised, at each x separately, by v=−g (complete the square: 21​∥v+g∥2−21​∥g∥2).

So each JKO step moves every bit of mass by about −τ∇W​f, and the staircase curve ατ​(t) converges to a curve whose mass moves with velocity vt​=−∇W​f(αt​). By the continuity equation (refresher), ∂t​αt​+div(αt​vt​)=0, that is

 ∂t​αt​=div(αt​∇δαδf​(αt​)) ​(OT4ML (15.4); StatOT Def. 5.14, p. 153).
How rigorous is this?

The book calls the argument formal: it assumes that the JKO minimiser is reached by a small optimal displacement and that f is smooth. The rigorous statement is a theorem about curves of maximal slope in metric spaces (OT4ML Defs. 15.8–15.9, pp. 359–360, after Ambrosio, Gigli and Savaré): under convexity, compactness and lower-semicontinuity assumptions, the staircase curves converge as τ→0, and the limit satisfies (15.4) when everything is smooth. Jordan, Kinderlehrer and Otto proved it in 1998 for the Fokker–Planck energy. On this page we use (15.4) as the definition of the Wasserstein gradient flow, as StatOT does.

A more precise version of “each step moves the mass by −τ∇W​f” uses the first variation of 21​W22​ computed in §3: if T is the optimal map from the new iterate α(ℓ+1) back to the old one, the optimality condition of the JKO step reads τT(x)−x​=∇W​f(α(ℓ+1))(x) — a particle that ends at x came from T(x), moving with the velocity −∇W​f evaluated at the end of the step: an implicit Euler step, exactly as in §1 (derived formally in the solution of Exercise 6, §13).

The energy always decreases: dissipation#

In the course StatOT (5.10), p. 153

A quick calculation using the definition of the Wasserstein gradient flow (μt​)t≥0​ of F yields

∂t​F(μt​)=⟨∇W​F(μt​),vt​⟩μt​​=−∥∇W​F(μt​)∥μt​2​(5.10)

where vt​=−∇W​F(μt​) is the tangent vector at time t. This equality, which states that the objective functional is dissipated at a rate equal to the squared norm of the gradient, is a generic fact about gradient flows.

  1. dtd​f(αt​)=∫δαδf​(αt​)∂t​αt​.
    First variation with the zero-mass perturbation ∂t​αt​dt (StatOT p. 152).
  2. =∫δαδf​div(αt​∇δαδf​)=−∫​∇δαδf​(αt​)​2dαt​ ≤0.
    The PDE, then one integration by parts. This is fact (1) of §1, lifted to measures: the energy decreases at the rate of the squared slope.
Worked example — the dissipation rate of a Fokker–Planck flow

Take f=KL(⋅∣N(0,1)) and α0​=N(2,0.52). From the refresher: f(α0​)=21​(0.25+4−1−log0.25)=2.3181 and the squared slope is the Fisher information I=m2+(s−s1​)2=4+(0.5−2)2=6.25. So the KL should start decreasing at the rate 6.25. With the exact solution of the next subsections (mt​=2e−t, st2​=1−0.75e−2t), a finite difference gives dtd​KL=−6.24998 at t=0. ✓

Potential energy: transport by −∇V#

In the course OT4ML Ex. 15.11, pp. 360–361

Example 15.11 (Linear potentials generate independent particles). Take a linear functional f(α)=∫h(x)dα(x). Then δf(α)=h is independent of α, and the flow (15.4) becomes ∂t∂αt​​+div(−∇hαt​)=0. This implies particles move independently according to the usual gradient flow (15.2).

Each particle follows x˙=−∇V(x) and ignores all the others: the flow is the push-forward of α0​ by the flow map of the ODE. Example V(x)=21​x2: x(t)=x0​e−t, so N(m,s2) becomes N(me−t,s2e−2t) — the measure shrinks towards the minimiser of V and concentrates (its limit is δ0​). There is no diffusion: a Dirac stays a Dirac (§2).

Entropy: the heat equation#

In the course OT4ML Ex. 15.13, p. 361

Example 15.13 (Entropy generates heat and porous-medium flows). The canonical density-dependent functional is the Shannon neg-entropy f(α)=∫log(dxdα​(x))dα(x). If α=ρdx, then δf(α)=logρ+1, up to an immaterial additive constant, so ∇W​f(α)=∇logρ is the score. The flow (15.4) becomes the heat equation ∂t​ρt​=Δρt​. […] For a generalized entropy f(ρdx)=∫g(ρ(x))dx with a scalar convex function g, one obtains nonlinear diffusions in the smooth-density regime: ∂t∂ρt​​=Δ(P(ρt​)), where the pressure P satisfies P′(s)=sg′′(s). For example, g(s)=slog(s) gives P(s)=s […], while g(s)=sm/(m−1), m>1, gives P(s)=sm up to an additive constant and yields the porous-medium equation.

  1. ∂t​ρ=div(ρ∇(logρ+1))=div(ρρ∇ρ​)=div(∇ρ)=Δρ.
    (15.4) with the first variation of the entropy; ρ∇logρ=∇ρ (refresher).
  2. For ∫g(ρ): ρ∇g′(ρ)=ρg′′(ρ)∇ρ=∇P(ρ) with P′(s)=sg′′(s), so ∂t​ρ=div(∇P(ρ))=ΔP(ρ).Chain rule. For g=slogs, g′′=1/s and P′=1; for g=sm/(m−1), P′(s)=msm−1, P=sm.

A diffusion without randomness. The heat flow from N(m,s2) is N(m,s2+2t). Read along particles: the velocity is −∇logρt​(x)=s2+2tx−m​, linear in x, and the particle starting at x0​ follows x(t)=m+(x0​−m)1+2t/s2​ — deterministic, and it never crosses another particle. With s2=0.25, the particle starting at x0​=1 is at 3 at t=1 (ODE solver: 3.000000). Particles spread because each one is pushed down the density, i.e. along minus the score. The random picture (Brownian particles with the same law) is §6.

Pitfall — a PDE does not determine its energy, nor its metric
In the course OT4ML Rem. 15.14, p. 361

The heat equation already illustrates that a PDE does not determine a unique gradient-flow structure. […] In the Hilbert geometry of densities, the squared distance and the Dirichlet energy are dL22​(α,β)=∫∣ρα​−ρβ​∣2dx, D(α)=21​∫∥∇ρ∥2dx, so δD/δρ=−Δρ and the L2 gradient flow ∂t​ρt​=−δD/δρ(ρt​) gives ∂t​ρt​=Δρt​. […] explaining a dynamics as a gradient flow requires specifying both an energy and a metric, and different pairs (f,d) may produce the same PDE.

“The heat equation is a gradient flow” is incomplete: of 21​∫∥∇ρ∥2 for L2 (it decreases oscillations), and of ∫ρlogρ for W2​ (it spreads mass). Exercise 2 of the sheet computes both pairs for two energies (§13). Only the transport reading extends to particles and gives the rates of §7.

Interaction energy: aggregation#

In the course OT4ML (15.9), pp. 361–362

Interaction energies. In a similar spirit, to obtain nonlinear evolutions without requiring the measure to have density, one can consider f(α):=∬k(x,y)dα(x)dα(y). (15.9) For a symmetric kernel k: δf(α)(x)=2∫k(x,y)dα(y), ∇W​f(α)(x)=2∫∇x​k(x,y)dα(y). For α0​=n1​∑i​δxi​​, the flow (15.4) implies particles (xi​(t))i​ obey: x˙i​(t)=−n2​∑j​∇k(xi​(t),xj​(t)).

Each particle is pushed by all the others, through the kernel; the velocity depends on the whole measure. A positive bump k (for example Gaussian) is repulsive (minimising ∬k wants particles far apart); a convex growing k such as ∥x−y∥2 is attractive. Worked example with the variance of §3, k=41​(x−y)2: the velocity is −(x−m), so x(t)=m+(x0​−m)e−t; the mean m is conserved and the variance decays like e−2t: the whole measure aggregates into the Dirac at its mean. Mixed kernels (repulsive at short range, attractive at long range) produce stable patterns — try them in the particle widget of §5.

KL to a Gibbs measure: the Fokker–Planck equation#

In the course OT4ML Ex. 15.15, (15.10), pp. 363–364

Example 15.15 (Langevin drift as a free-energy flow). If b=−∇V, this linear Fokker–Planck equation [∂t​ρt​=−div(bρt​)+σ2Δρt​] is the W2​ gradient flow of the free energy ρ↦∫Vρdx+σ2∫ρlogρdx. […] For a prescribed target β=ρβ​dx, take b=σ2∇logρβ​. The SDE, the Fokker–Planck equation, and the deterministic continuity equation with score velocity are then three representations of the same gradient flow:

∂t​ρt​=σ2div(ρt​∇logρβ​ρt​​),vt​=σ2(∇logρβ​−∇logρt​).(15.10)
free energy
Potential energy plus σ2 times the neg-entropy. With σ=1 and ρβ​=Z−1e−V it is KL(α∣β) up to the constant logZ.
σ2
The temperature: the strength of the diffusion. Below, σ=1.
vt​
The velocity of the mass: towards higher target density (∇logρβ​=−∇V), away from higher current density (−∇logρt​). It vanishes exactly when ρt​∝ρβ​: the Gibbs measure is the stationary state.
“three representations”
The PDE, the Langevin SDE (§6) and the deterministic particles x˙=vt​(x): three descriptions of the same curve of measures.

With σ=1: ∂t​ρ=div(ρ∇(logρ+V))=Δρ+div(ρ∇V) — the Fokker–Planck equation. Example (Ornstein–Uhlenbeck): V=21​x2, β=N(0,1). From N(m,s2), the velocity −x+st2​x−mt​​ is affine in x, so the law stays Gaussian (§9) with m˙=−m and dtd​s2=2(1−s2):

αt​=N(me−t, 1+(s2−1)e−2t).

From N(2,0.52): at t=1, α1​=N(0.7358, 0.8985). The mean relaxes like e−t, the variance like e−2t, towards N(0,1).

In machine learning — scores

The Wasserstein gradient of the neg-entropy is the score ∇logρ, and the velocity of every flow containing an entropy involves the score of the current law. Scores can be learned from samples without knowing ρ: score matching (Hyvärinen, 2005) and denoising score matching (Vincent, 2011) fit a network sθ​(x)≈∇logρ(x) by least squares (both cited in OT4ML §16.1, p. 407). With a learned score, the particles x˙=−∇V(x)−sθ​(x) simulate a Fokker–Planck flow without any noise; run backwards in time, the same idea generates data (§6). Diffusion models are built on exactly this pair of objects: a Fokker–Planck flow towards N(0,Id) and the score along it.

Reflexes
  • ∂t​α=div(α∇δαδf​) → read it on particles: x˙=−∇δαδf​(αt​)(x).
  • div(ρ∇logρ)=Δρ → an entropy in the energy means a Laplacian in the PDE.
  • Stationary states of a Wasserstein gradient flow → the first variation is constant on the support (∇δαδf​=0 there): for KL, ρ∝e−V.
  • Gaussian data and an affine velocity → the flow stays Gaussian; write ODEs for (m,s2).

Which energy has the flow ∂t​ρ=div(ρ(x−mˉ)) on R, where mˉ is a fixed number? And ∂t​ρ=div(ρ(x−m(ρ))) with m(ρ)=∫xρ?

Answer

The first: velocity −(x−mˉ)=−∇V with V=21​(x−mˉ)2, a potential energy ∫Vdα; mass contracts to mˉ. The second: velocity −(x−m(ρ)), the gradient of 21​(x−m)2, which is the first variation of 41​∬(x−y)2dαdα (up to a constant): an interaction energy, aggregation to the conserved mean. Same instantaneous velocity field, different energies: the first “knows” where mˉ is, the second only sees the measure.

5. Particles and densities: Lagrangian and Eulerian flows OT4ML (15.5), p. 360#

Started from n Diracs, a Wasserstein gradient flow stays a sum of n Diracs whose positions solve x˙i​=−∇W​f(αt​)(xi​)=−n∇xi​​F(X): plain gradient descent on the positions, n times faster; densities on a grid (Eulerian) and moving particles (Lagrangian) are two discretisations of the same equation, and only the second one is dimension-free — provided the energy makes sense on a point cloud.

Particles follow the Wasserstein gradient#

In the course OT4ML §15.1, (15.5), p. 360

Discrete evolutions. If f admits a first variation whose spatial gradient is well defined at empirical measures, the characteristic form of (15.4) preserves the number and weights of the atoms. For equal weights, write αt​=n1​∑i​δxi​(t)​. The particles X(t):=(xi​(t))i​ evolve according to the coupled ODEs

x˙i​(t)=−n∇xi​​F(X(t)),(15.5)

where F(X):=f(n1​∑i​δxi​​) and the factor n comes from the empirical Wasserstein metric n1​∑i​∥x˙i​∥2.

“characteristic form”
The continuity equation moves mass along the curves x˙=vt​(x) (its characteristics). Starting from atoms, each atom simply follows its own characteristic: the number of atoms and their weights never change.
F(X)
The energy, seen as an ordinary function of the nd coordinates of the particles. Example: f=∫Vdα gives F(X)=n1​∑i​V(xi​).
−n∇xi​​F
The usual gradient of F with respect to the position of particle i, multiplied by n.
n1​∑i​∥x˙i​∥2
The kinetic energy ∫∥v∥2dα of the motion when each particle carries mass n1​: the Wasserstein metric on configurations. A gradient for the metric n1​∥⋅∥2 is n times the Euclidean gradient.

Why n∇xi​​F(X)=∇W​f(α)(xi​). Move particle i alone by εu. This moves the mass n1​ sitting at xi​ with velocity u, so by Proposition 15.7 the energy changes at the rate ∫⟨∇W​f,v⟩dα=n1​⟨∇W​f(α)(xi​),u⟩. Hence ∇xi​​F(X)=n1​∇W​f(α)(xi​), and (15.5) is the Wasserstein flow evaluated at the particles. Check on the example of §3, f=21​Var and X=(0,1,5): F(X)=21​⋅31​∑i​(xi​−xˉ)2, so ∇xi​​F=31​(xi​−xˉ) and 3∇xi​​F=xi​−xˉ=(−2,−1,3), the Wasserstein gradient found in §3. ✓

Pitfall — gradient descent on positions has a different clock

Automatic differentiation of a loss F(X) written as a function of the positions returns ∇xi​​F=n1​∇W​f(xi​). Gradient descent X←X−τ∇F(X) therefore follows the Wasserstein flow with the time step τ/n: same trajectories, n times slower. To compare runs with different numbers of particles, multiply the learning rate by n (equivalently, differentiate nF instead of F).

Two ways to discretise a flow#

In the course CompOT Rem. 9.12, pp. 155–156

Remark 9.12 (Lagrangian discretization using particles systems). The finite-dimensional problem in (9.26) can be interpreted as the Eulerian discretization of a flow over the space of measures (9.27). An alternative way to discretize the problem, using the so-called Lagrangian method using particles systems, is to parameterize instead the solution as a (discrete) empirical measure moving with time, where the locations of that measure (and not its weights) become the variables of interest. […] If the energy F is finite for discrete measures, then one can simply define F(X)=F(n1​∑i=1n​δxi​​). […] For functions such as generalized entropy, which are only finite for measures having densities, one should apply a density estimator to convert the point cloud into a density […].

Eulerian (densities on a grid)Lagrangian (moving particles)
unknownsthe mass in each fixed cellthe positions of n atoms of fixed mass
equationthe PDE ∂t​ρ=div(ρ∇δαδf​)the ODEs x˙i​=−∇δαδf​(αt​)(xi​)
costgrows like h−d for a mesh size h: hopeless beyond d=3n particles in any dimension; O(n2) for pairwise interactions
entropy, KL, Fishernatural (densities are available)+∞ on point clouds: needs noise (§6), a density estimate, or a kernel (§9)
potential, interaction, MMD, W2​, Sinkhornpossibleexact: the particle flow is the Wasserstein flow of the empirical measure

Machine learning lives in high dimension, so it uses the Lagrangian picture almost exclusively: the particles are samples, neurons or tokens (§8–§11). The JKO widget of §2 was already Lagrangian (particles at quantile levels), in one dimension where the entropy can be written with the gaps between neighbours.

Mean-field limit

When the velocity of each particle depends on the empirical measure of all of them, the system is a mean-field interacting particle system (StatOT §5.8, p. 165: “each particle interacts with the others only through the effect of their distribution, and these interactions have the same form for all the particles”). If the initial empirical measures converge to a density α0​, the particle flows converge to the solution of the PDE started at α0​: n particles are a Monte Carlo approximation of the flow. With noise, this is propagation of chaos and the limit is the McKean–Vlasov equation (OT4ML p. 364).

Interacting particles: aggregation and patterns#

Interaction energies f(α)=21​∬W(x−y)dα(x)dα(y) (StatOT’s normalisation, gradient ∫∇W(x−y)dα(y)) are finite on point clouds, so their particle flows x˙i​=−n1​∑j=i​∇W(xi​−xj​) are exact. Attraction at long range and repulsion at short range produce stable shapes.

Worked example — attraction and Coulomb repulsion make a uniform disk

In R2, let W(z)=21​∥z∥2−log∥z∥: quadratic attraction, logarithmic (Coulomb) repulsion. Claim: the equilibrium is the uniform probability on a disk of radius 1 (density π1​).

  1. At an equilibrium, ∇W​f=0 on the support, so δαδf​(x)=∫W(x−y)dα(y) is constant there.Stationary states of a gradient flow (§4 reflex).
  2. Δx​21​∥x−y∥2=2 and Δx​(−log∥x−y∥)=−2πδy​ in R2.Δ21​∥x∥2=d=2; −2π1​log∥x∥ is the fundamental solution of −Δ in the plane.
  3. 0=Δδαδf​(x)=∫(2−2πδy​(x))dα(y)=2−2πρ(x) inside the support.Apply the Laplacian to the constant of line 1, inside the support; line 2.
  4. ρ=π1​ on the support, which has area π since the mass is 1: a disk of radius 1 (centred at the conserved mean).Rotation invariance of the problem; uniqueness of the equilibrium is admitted.

Check with particles. With 300 particles and explicit steps 0.01 up to t=10 (the widget below, “Coulomb” preset), the largest distance to the mean is 0.97, and the fractions of particles within 0.5 and 0.75 of the mean are 0.25 and 0.56 — the uniform disk gives 0.25 and 0.5625.

Interactive figure (needs JavaScript).

What to look at: press Run. The orange-red dots are the initial cloud, the green dots the particles at time t, the black circle their mean (conserved by every interaction energy: the forces between two particles are opposite). The curve on the right is the energy f(αt​), which can only decrease (§4). “Attraction”: the cloud collapses onto its mean (aggregation; the energy 21​Var decays like e−2t). “Coulomb”: it settles into the uniform unit disk of the worked example (compare the radial fractions with 0.25 and 0.5625). “Gaussian repulsion”: short-range repulsion and quadratic attraction balance into a flat disk with a denser rim. “Potential”: an external potential pulls the particles onto the unit circle and the repulsion spreads them evenly around it.

In machine learning — particles are the parameters

Every system of this lesson where “the loss depends on a population” is an interacting particle system: generated samples fitted to data by an MMD (§8), neurons of a wide network (§10: the risk is a quadratic interaction between neurons plus a potential), tokens in a transformer (§11: attention is a normalised interaction), sampling particles in SVGD (§9). Equation (15.5) says that training such a system by gradient descent on the particles is, up to the factor n, a Wasserstein gradient flow of the population — which is what allows one to analyse it as a PDE when n is large (the “mean-field limit”).

Reflexes
  • Particles of mass n1​ → x˙i​=−∇W​f(xi​)=−n∇xi​​F(X).
  • Energy infinite on point clouds (entropy) → add noise (Langevin), estimate a density, or kernelise (SVGD).
  • Interaction energies conserve the mean of the particles (action = reaction).

Two particles on R at x1​=−1, x2​=1, with W(z)=21​z2 (so f=41​∬(x−y)2dαdα). Write their ODEs and solve them.

Answer

x˙1​=−21​(x1​−x2​), x˙2​=−21​(x2​−x1​) (the sum over j=i has one term, divided by n=2). The mean 0 is conserved and the gap g=x2​−x1​ solves g˙​=−g, so x1,2​(t)=∓e−t. Same as the Wasserstein flow of §4: x˙=−(x−m).
